item.title: Rogers seeks to offset hit from CRTC fee ban as wireless service revenue dips in Q3
item.description: Rogers Communications Inc. says it is seeking to offset the hit it has taken from the CRTC’s recent ban on telecommunications carriers charging certain administrative fees.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Rogers Communications Inc. says it is seeking to offset the hit it has taken from the CRTC’s recent ban on telecommunications carriers charging certain administrative fees. While Rogers reported a year-over-year increase in overall revenue during its most recent quarter, primarily due to growth in its media division, the company said wireless service revenue decreased one per cent. During its third quarter, Rogers’ mobile phone average monthly revenue per user was $55.22, down from $56.70 in the same quarter of the prior year. Chief financial officer Glenn Brandt said the “largest impact” to that closely watched figure came from the CRTC’s move in June to prohibit telecoms from charging customers when they activate, change or cancel plans. “The purpose of those setup fees was exactly that — to offset costs of account changes or new accounts coming on,” Brandt told analysts on a conference call Friday. “The charge disappeared (due to) the CRTC decision. The costs don’t.” He said Rogers put in place some “early initiatives” during the quarter to recover some of those costs, but “there’s still more work to do.” “We’re now moving back to finding alternatives for covering those costs, shipping costs, for example … so that effort remains ongoing.” The CRTC has said the new rules are meant to make it easier for customers to switch internet and cellphone plans without having to worry about unexpected charges. The regulator is in the midst of a review into whether Rogers, along with rivals Bell Canada and Telus Corp., violated the ban by introducing new fees around the time it took effect. It said Rogers began charging customers a $40 device setup fee, $25 shipping charge, and an unspecified SIM card fee in mid-June that “would not appear” to qualify for an exemption under the rules for optional services or products that consumers consent to purchase. Rogers has argued the device setup fee is related to an optional purchase. It also said the shipping and SIM fees were not new, and that the latter is only charged when a customer replaces a lost or damaged SIM, rather than at activation. Overall, the quarter saw a “less active telecom market,” said Rogers president and CEO Tony Staffieri said, as the company reported a profit attributable to shareholders of $482 million. “In wireless, we stayed focused on financials versus chasing subscriber volume in what is typically a busy back-to-school quarter,” he told analysts. The company reported 17,000 total mobile phone net subscriber additions, including 6,000 postpaid — those who pay a monthly bill for their wireless services after charges have accumulated. That was down from 62,000 postpaid additions in the same quarter last year. Rogers’ monthly churn — a measure of those who cancelled their service — for net postpaid mobile subscribers was 1.03 per cent, up from 0.99 per cent during its previous third quarter. Retail internet net additions totalled 10,000, down from 29,000 a year earlier. The company said its profit amounted to 88 cents per diluted share for the quarter ended Sept. 30. The result compared with a profit of $5.71 billion or $10.54 per diluted share a year ago when it saw a $5-billion non-cash gain related to its stake in Maple Leaf Sports & Entertainment and $151-million gain on the redemption of long-term debt. On an adjusted basis, Rogers said it earned $704 million in net income, or $1.29 per diluted share in its latest quarter, down from an adjusted profit of $1.37 per diluted share a year ago. Revenue totalled $5.44 billion, up from $5.35 billion in the same quarter last year. “Financial results were in line with our forecast while subscriber growth was a little lighter than our forecast,” said RBC analyst Drew McReynolds in a note. “We view the results as largely neutral for the shares at current levels.” Earlier this month, Rogers completed its $4.35-billion purchase of the remaining 25 per cent stake in MLSE it did not already hold, giving it complete ownership of the sports conglomerate that includes the Maple Leafs, Raptors, Toronto FC and Argonauts. Staffieri reiterated Rogers’ plan to sell a minority interest in its consolidated sports, media and entertainment portfolio to third-party investors, adding he remains “bullish about our plan to unlock shareholder value and drive long-term growth.” Rogers is targeting the first half of 2027 to close that minority interest sale. “Investor interest in these assets is substantial as sports franchise valuations continue to rise,” Staffieri said. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026. By Sammy Hudes BNN Bloomberg, CTV News and CP24 are owned by Bell Media, which is a division of BCE.

item.title: Statistics Canada reports retail sales up 1.2% in August at $74.6 billion
item.description: Statistics Canada says retail sales rose 1.2 per cent to $74.6 billion in August, helped by higher new car sales.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA — Statistics Canada says retail sales rose 1.2 per cent to $74.6 billion in August, helped by higher new car sales. The agency says sales were up in all nine of the subsectors it tracks, led by increases at motor vehicle and parts dealers which gained 1.2 per cent, boosted by a 1.5 per cent rise at new car dealers. Core retail sales, which exclude gasoline stations and fuel vendors and motor vehicle and parts dealers, were up 1.1 per cent for the month. The food and beverage retailers subsector gained 1.1 per cent, while general merchandise retailers added one per cent. In volume terms, overall retail sales rose 1.2 per cent in August. Looking ahead, Statistics Canada says its advance estimate of retail sales in September suggested a gain of 0.7 per cent for the month, though it cautioned the figure would be revised. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

item.title: Wall Street loses ground under pressure from rising oil prices, more swings for Big Tech stocks
item.description: Futures are lower as oil prices reach levels not seen since May amid halting efforts to bring the U.S. and Iran back to the negotiation table.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — Stocks slipped on Wall Street Friday under increasing pressure from rising oil prices. The S&P 500 fell 0.2 per cent, adding to its decline from a day before. The index is on track for a second-straight week of losses. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 541 points, or 1 per cent, as of 11:12 a.m. Eastern time. The Nasdaq composite rose 0.2 per cent, bolstered by gains for several big tech stocks that also helped ease losses elsewhere. Rising oil prices weighed heavily on the broader market, where three out of every four stocks within the benchmark S&P 500 index fell. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.4 per cent to $115.86. It has surged from less than $97 at the start of October and is now at its highest level since March. Several AI-related companies made big moves. Micron Technology jumped 3.4 per cent and Microsoft rose 0.8 per cent and helped ease the impact on major indexes from a broad drop for most stocks. Even a relatively small 0.3 per cent gain from Nvidia went a long way to help offset losses elsewhere in the market. The tech sector’s influence is also capable of quickly switching over to a heavy weight. Stocks that have benefited from the frenzy over AI have been swinging over rising worries about their path ahead. Investors are worried about whether their high prices are justified. Many of those companies have been borrowing to fund investments in AI technology and high interest rates are making those loans more expensive. The latest round of corporate earnings are being closely-watched to help get a better sense of whether those investments are paying off, or might pay off. Several influential AI-related companies report their latest financial results next week, including Google’s parent, Alphabet, along with Microsoft and Amazon. Industrial companies had some of the broadest losses. Caterpillar slumped 2.3 per cent and Boeing fell 1 per cent. American Express slumped 3.3 per cent and joined a drop for other financial companies, despite r eporting profits for its most recent quarter that beat analysts’ forecasts. The company did announce its first major job cuts in roughly a decade. Rising oil prices that weighed down much of the market helped boost energy companies. Chevron rose 2.4 per cent and ConocoPhillips rose 4.2 per cent. European markets were lower. France’s main index fell 0.7 per cent, though yields on French government bonds eased a bit. Treasury yields in the U.S. edged higher following sharp drops on Thursday. The yield on the 10-year Treasury edged up to 4.99 per cent from 4.96 per cent late Thursday. Yields have been rising globally, partly over worries about governments taking on too much debt. Inflation also remains a concern and is stubbornly well above 3 per cent in the U.S. That prompted the Federal Reserve to raise its benchmark interest rate at its last meeting in an effort to cool inflation. Wall Street expects the central bank to hold rates steady at its meeting next week, but is leaning heavily toward another rate hike in December. Wall Street will also get several big economic updates next week, including the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation. The personal consumption expenditures index, or PCE, is expected to show that inflation rose at a 3.6 per cent rate in September, sharply above the Fed’s 2 per cent target. The U.S. war with Iran has severely cut the world’s oil supply, driving energy prices higher and fueling a sharp jump in the cost of everything from gasoline to food and clothes. --- Damian J. Troise, The Associated Press

item.title: Dale Jackson: Canadian investors are not as diversified as they think, survey finds
item.description: A new survey commissioned by Picton Investments and conducted by Pollara Strategic Insights found 83 per cent of Canadian investors are confident their portfolios are well diversified. But are they?
item.content:encoded:
A new survey commissioned by Picton Investments and conducted by Pollara Strategic Insights found 83 per cent of Canadian investors are confident their portfolios are well diversified. Yet only 57 per cent say they are familiar with a structural shift in global equity markets that concentrates fewer companies in major stock market indices such as the S&P 500.

The report suggests investors are unaware of the risk associated with the growing market weight of a small number of large companies – many tied to technology and artificial intelligence – in the same indices used as benchmarks for mutual funds and exchange traded funds (ETFs). It notes Canadian investors predominantly rely on traditional investment products including mutual funds (55 per cent) and ETFs (31 per cent). Canadian investors especially vulnerable Diversification hedges risk by strategically spreading portfolio assets among sectors, geographic regions and asset classes. It also exposes the portfolio to a wide variety of opportunity. The Picton report also points out Canadian investors could be especially at risk due to what is termed “home-country bias.” A 2024 report from Vanguard found Canadian investment portfolios are 18 times overweight in their Canadian holdings; increasing exposure to domestic risks and decreasing exposure to a world of opportunity outside our borders. According to the report, Canadian securities account for about half of Canadian portfolios despite the fact that Canadian securities account for under three per cent of the global market. Of that tiny sliver of global securities, roughly two-thirds of the stocks listed on Canada’s Toronto Stock Exchange are tied to the finance and resource sectors. The report also found the top ten holdings in Canada constitute more than 38 per cent of the S&P/TSX index, compared with 12 per cent of the global market. The right mix for the right portfolio The good news, according to the Vanguard report, is that Canadian investors are gradually reducing levels of home bias from 67 per cent in 2012. The trend is likely a holdover from before the 1990s when registered retirement savings plans (RRSPs) were restricted to 30 per cent foreign holdings. Vanguard says a more balanced investment portfolio for Canadians would hold 30 per cent Canadian equities and 70 per cent international equities. However, that weighting could be different for individuals, such as snowbirds, if they spend more of their retirement dollars outside Canada. How to achieve global diversification in your portfolio While it’s important for Canadian portfolios to diversify beyond Canada, it is just as important to diversify among foreign holdings. That means including a wide array of sectors and geographic regions. There are many ways for retail investors to get access to foreign equities but the cost of dealing in foreign currencies is a hidden risk many don’t consider. How to build an investment portfolio that can weather uncertainty Most foreign equity funds sold in Canada have a version that hedges the Canadian dollar at a cost much higher than the U.S. dollar version. To avoid having to pay currency traders for an ongoing labyrinth of foreign transactions, it’s best to buy foreign equities in U.S. dollars, which is the global standard currency. That means banking up U.S. dollars in trading accounts such as RRSPs and tax-free savings accounts (TFSAs). There are three basic ways for Canadians to invest globally: 1. Global and international mutual funds Most Canadian mutual fund providers offer a wide variety of global funds including broad global funds (all countries), international funds (all countries minus Canada and the U.S.), or funds that concentrate on specific countries, regions, or global sectors like technology. Many foreign equity funds are actively managed by investment teams with vast research capabilities and experience in the focus area. Some funds are sub-managed by firms located in the specific geographic region. Annual fees for that sort of reach and expertise can top three per cent of the total amount invested, which is ultimately drawn from the total return. 2. Global exchange traded funds ETFs generally have the same reach as mutual funds in terms of geographic regions and global sectors. The big difference is; they are passively managed. That means holdings are bought and sold according to a preset formula such as market weighting in the underlying index. ETFs are not as effective as actively managed mutual funds at adjusting to changes or nuances relating to specific foreign markets. On the plus side, fees on unhedged foreign ETFs are usually much lower than mutual funds; often below 0.05 per cent on the amount invested annually. Market weighted ETFs that track an index are also more transparent. Holdings and changes mimic the underlying index while mutual fund managers are only required to provide scant information on what and how much the fund holds. 3. U.S. listed stocks Stocks trading on overseas markets can be difficult for the average investor to buy directly but most Canadian trading accounts offer full access to major U.S. exchanges. U.S. equities are also global equities because roughly 50 per cent of all publicly traded companies in the world are based in the United States. Many generate revenue and grow earnings around the world. That not only gives investors in U.S. stocks a global reach, but it also puts the onus on the company to hedge all other foreign currencies.
